Born 29 Apr 1912 at Sutherlin, Oregon, the second child of George F. Adams, pharmacist, and Serena Trumbo. Her birth certificate is marked "ALTERED": her given names, Edith Van Tyne, were added later by affidavit. Van Tyne is her grandmother Mary Frances Vantine's surname.

In 1930 she was 17, a stepdaughter in Arthur T. Wells's household at Burlingame. She married Thomas White Childs about 1934 (married 16 years in 1950); they lived in Philadelphia in 1935 and in Portland, Oregon, from 1940, with their sons George C. and Gregg E. Childs. She died on 10 May 2000 and was buried beside Thomas at Willamette National Cemetery.

She married Thomas White Childs on Monday, 11 Sep 1933, at St. Paul's Episcopal Church, Burlingame. The Salem Statesman Journal (9 Sep 1933) called her "Miss Edith Adams, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. A. T. Wells of Burlingame, Calif., and niece of Mr. and Mrs. E. Hanzlick of Portland", well known in Portland; the couple left at once for Philadelphia.
She and Thomas returned from Philadelphia to Portland in June 1936 (Daily Capital Journal, 23 Jun 1936). Their niche marker at Willamette National Cemetery reads "Edith Adams, 1912–2000".

people.name: Joseph Pierre Jose Adams (Jose2)
locations: Fairmount Cemetery, Denver, Denver County, CO
notable_stories: Freighted with mule trains up the Arkansas River to Denver in 1863
He was active in moving the Douglas County seat to Castle Rock

In 1863 he took the train to St. Joe and stage to Leavenworth, then hired on as a six-yoke ox-team driver on the Santa Fe trail; at Larned, Kansas Comanches attacked the camp, killed the wagon master and took the oxen, and troops from the Larned post rescued the party the next day.

While in office he helped secure construction of the Castle Rock courthouse (only $14,000 of $20,000 in voted bonds was needed) and was active in moving the county seat from Frenchtown to Castle Rock.

As a boy during the Civil War he left unsettled Missouri in 1863, went to St. Joe and Leavenworth, and hired on as a driver of a six-yoke ox team to Santa Fe. At Larned, Kansas, Comanches attacked the camp, fought all afternoon, killed the wagon master and took the oxen; government troops from the Larned post rescued the party the next day.
He stated that his grandfather died of accidental poisoning, and the grandfather's newly found obituary confirms it.

notable_stories: Signed a spelling paper for her mother in second grade and was punished for it.
Accidentally launched a pencil with a rubber band into the principal’s habit in fourth grade.
Lipsynced in choir to avoid singing and was removed for singing off key.
Fell onto Sister Angela while sliding down a railing and knocked off her headpiece.
Gave Andrew Pulaski a black eye after he kept snapping her bra straps on a crowded bus.
She says she became an encyclopedia on Abraham Lincoln and made her father take her to the Lincoln Memorial, the Smithsonian, and Gettysburg.
She reflects that she did not grow up hearing stories about her birth because her mother died when she was very young and men were not allowed in the delivery room.
Remembers the circus as her earliest memory.
Was the best bowler of her league and age group and qualified for Duckpins for Dollars.
Hated being called Babs or Babsie by her father’s family and would cringe when her aunts used it.
Hit or pinched Chuck when he called her Babs, often trying to catch him when he ran.
Beat up her brother’s friends if they called her Babs, and says Tommy Dudek was a slow learner.
Near her eleventh birthday, she shared birthday parties with Chuck because her beloved grandfather died around that time.
Remembered her grandfather as her best friend growing up and described outings with him, including Veteran’s Day poppies, doughnuts, magic tricks, poetry, piano playing, and babysitting.
Lost a Super Bowl lunch bet to Lowell Tiller and sent him a peanut butter and jelly sack lunch by way of John during a Reserve weekend.
Won a later Super Bowl bet by choosing the 49ers because she liked Joe Montana and received a catered lunch from Henry’s at St. Rose School.
Collected baseball cards from Yankees players of the 1950s and 1960s.
Remembered the Yankees as the Orioles’ nemesis and Memorial Stadium selling out when they came to town.
Remembered her dad taking the family to many Colts games at Memorial Stadium.
On the first day of first grade, she followed Chuck onto the boys’ side of the bus and then into the boys’ bathroom, which led to her being sent to the principal’s office.

She says that first-grade incident began a long pattern of visits to the principal’s office for later incidents including the pencil incident, playground incident, banister incident, confession incident, black eye incident, Brownie incident, and signature incident.
She says she and others used to steal peaches from the blind school.
She rode home from the park with her coat saturated in blood after almost bleeding to death.
She says Fred the gerbil was sucked up in the vacuum.
Spent long summer days outside until dinner time and school days outside from three o’clock until dinner.
Skated through the neighborhood after dinner while adults sat on porches.
Climbed in the quarry, climbed trees, stole peaches from the blind school, waded in streams for crawdads, and played baseball.
Once chased a flasher and threw rocks at him.
Spent Sundays at her grandmother’s house with cousins, sometimes all day and into the night.
Explored Herring Run Park with cousins.
Entered Mercy High and had to make new friends after not sharing classes with Louise and Jeanne.
Ran in a close-knit pack of friends throughout all four years of high school.
Performed in school plays including The Wizard of Oz, Alibaba And the 40 Thieves, Peter Pan, and Alice In Wonderland.
Relied mainly on the transit system to get to and from school.
Stayed friends with the same group at Towson State College.
Graduated early in December because of summer classes and married in January.
Lost touch with many of her high school friends after becoming a Navy wife.
Was a sophomore at Mercy High School when the announcement came over the intercom that President Kennedy had been shot.
Went with the whole school to the gym to say a rosary for him because the chapel was too small.
Stayed glued to the TV all weekend after Kennedy’s death.
Cried when John-John saluted his father’s casket.
Remembered visiting the state house in Annapolis because of her great uncle Teddy’s political role.
Met Brooks Robinson and Gus Triandos, and Gus Triandos signed her baseball card.
Talked to Johnny Unitas at the Golden Arm restaurant and to Alan Ameche when he came out to the car at one of his drive-ins.
Left class to investigate an unusual school announcement and unexpectedly encountered George Harrison and John Lennon in the hallway at Mercy High School.
Received detention for a week after being caught outside class during the Beatles visit, but felt it was worth it.
Saw Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel perform up close in a small auditorium at Towson State.
Was turned down by several department stores before getting an interview at Hochschild Kohn after her dad called Uncle Ted McKeldin.
Worked under the scrutiny of Mrs. Grey, who repeatedly reminded her how she got the job and seemed to wait for her to make mistakes.
Became a model employee because she felt fortunate to have the job and did not want to let Uncle Teddy down.
Grew up in Maryland and took many school field trips to major historical and civic sites.
Entered college with an open mind and initially considered veterinary medicine.
Was captivated by a Western Civilization professor who made history feel alive through vivid detail, including descriptions of Maria Antoinette and court life.
Declared History as her major because of that professor’s influence.
Completed a double major in Social Studies that included economics, psychology, political science, sociology, and geography.
Took summer classes all three years, mostly in English and science.
Became fascinated by flowers, shrubs, and trees after taking a Botany class in the summer.
Used a family vacation to Lake Chelan as part of the research for her master’s thesis on the history of Washington State.
Towed a boat around Washington for her SPU master’s class while visiting lakes and museums.
Tracked the path of the ancient Columbia River during the research trip.
Had to defend her thesis in her advisor’s office with only the advisor present and felt she got off easy.
Was raised between two brothers, many male first cousins, and boy neighbors, which taught her to stick up for herself.
Bloodied a few noses while defending herself and earned a reputation for being competitive and willful.
Had only two play dates with a girly-girl who lived two blocks away, and they did not go well.
Told her children that if they needed an instant decision, her answer would be no because she needed time to think.
Says her priorities shifted from self-development as a student to flexibility as a Navy wife and then to serving the needs of her children and grandchildren.
Says Marie took Chuck and her into her home when they were young.
Was present when Marie died on Barbara's birthday, February 12th.
Delivered a eulogy for Marie at the family luncheon after her death.
Describes Catholicism as woven into everyday life while growing up in Maryland.
Maintained church attendance through many moves during Navy life.
Made John stop in Tucson on a Sunday morning while moving from Beeville to San Diego so they could attend church.
Felt more at home with church involvement while living in Kelso.
Describes becoming more focused on Catholicism again in retirement and says she has come full circle.
Watched the assassination coverage on television.
Remembered Walter Cronkite interrupting the evening news.
Watched MLK's funeral on television.
Says the event did not affect her as deeply as JFK's assassination and funeral.
Watched the moon landing on television and found it amazing.
Followed news coverage of Neil Armstrong over the next six months.
Spent Army-Navy weekend in Philadelphia under close family chaperoning.
Was left alone with John in two connecting hotel rooms after the adults returned to Washington State, and they discussed marriage for the first time.
Went diamond shopping with John in Annapolis.
Recalls John proposing in the basement of her house.
Says they have been married 52 years and that he still makes her laugh.
Describes repeatedly taking whatever jobs were available while married to a Naval Aviator.
Worked day shifts while John flew nights in Florida, with the two of them switching seats in the car.
Lived in unfinished housing in Beeville and helped refurbish homes while cooking on a one-burner hot plate.
Found a successful teaching approach in Meridian by using Archie Manning as a bridge topic across racial division in the classroom.
Helped form a preschool in Port Townsend and later volunteered in Brian's classroom in Gilroy.
Built a long career path through St. Rose School, Lower Columbia College, Shasta Community College, University of Portland, and Crownpoint.
Designed a movie course in Crownpoint after polling students, and it became very popular.
Resigned in Crownpoint after repeated vandalism and lack of administrative support, and later regretted ending her career that way.
Worked as a substitute for the Ridgefield School district until the pandemic shut schools down.
Entered the hospital with a list of names and strongly wanted to avoid nicknames.
Says Brian was the only first name she and John both liked.
Chose John as Brian's middle name without argument.
Says she and John both picked Brendan before the hospital for their second son.
Chose McKeldin together as Brendan's middle name because it was her family name.
Wanted Brian and Brendan to know their grandparents, get a good education, be raised in the Catholic faith, and have fun.
Recalls Brendan trying to run away from home at his third birthday party in Ocean City after being sent for a timeout.
Describes repeated family travel for museums, historic sites, skiing, camping, rafting, and theme parks.
Drove with the boys to Disneyland to meet the Hinns and was scolded by a hotel manager after the boys bounced on the bed.
Says she took her master's degree credits at Seattle Pacific University while Nana and Papa helped with child care.
Says her heart overflowed with love when Brian met Brendan through the hospital window.
Remembers cheering both boys on for their rolling over, crawling, and first steps.
Describes a disastrous cross-country road trip from Meridian, Mississippi to San Diego, California with one-year-old Brian.
Recalls Brian's diaper blowout on the road, which led to leaving his ruined clothes and shoes on the roadside.
Recalls the car getting tar all over it from a freshly paved road, followed by paint stripping at the car wash.
Describes staying at the Navy Lodge while John attended Survival School.
Says this first trip with Brian was rough, but later trips with kids were happier.
Heard Brendan scream after being burned and immediately removed his pajamas and rushed him to the hospital.
Was restrained by hospital staff who suspected child abuse and questioned her for thirty minutes.
Felt shocked that she was suspected and described California as a strange place.
Later chose to have John take Brian to the hospital after a separate injury to avoid suspicion.
Agreed to co-coach her younger son's soccer team with Rich Hickey.
Realized early that neither the coach nor players understood soccer.
Went to the library and studied soccer techniques to prepare for practice.
Developed structured drills and skills training for the team.
Continued coaching for years until her son reached high school.
Received her mother’s jewelry as a surprise gift from her father on her 21st birthday.
Recounted multiple near-danger incidents involving her sons, including ferry, earthquake, and injury events.
Describes ongoing anxiety related to Brendan’s ferry incident even decades later.
Worked while commuting to college and did not live on campus.
Carefully selected professors based on reputation and expectations.
Felt both excited and nervous when Brian left for college.
Cried when dropping Brian off at the dorm.
Felt reassured by Brian’s independence and prior travel experience.
Worked at Pen Bay Laboratories in a tense specimen-cataloging role that required precision.
Lived in harsh conditions in Beeville while finishing unfinished houses and dealing with wildlife and limited utilities.
Taught in Meridian during desegregation and used Archie Manning as a unifying classroom topic.
Described motherhood as deeply changing her and centered her life around Brian and Brendan.
Enjoyed being a stay-at-home mother in Port Townsend and playing with her children.
Volunteered and taught in Gilroy while building new friendships and routines.
Worked under demanding conditions at St. Rose School and compared it to Pen Bay Laboratories.
Learned valuable lessons from Cambodian students at Lower Columbia College.
Joined a small book club in Redding and maintained friendships there.
Worked in recruiting and coordination for the University of Portland master's program, including travel to Canada and Guam.
Returned to Lower Columbia College as Running Start Coordinator and learned budgeting and counseling skills.
Described herself as SuperMom and SuperWife while managing work, sports, skiing, teenagers, and household responsibilities largely on her own.
Followed a strict diet while skiing with the boys at Mt. Hood.
Was taken out of a soccer game by coach Frank after nearly retaliating against an opposing player.
Threatened to quit her job and personally shadow Brian at school unless he improved his academics.
Went to war with Brendan's teacher after the teacher accused Brendan of trying to take over the class.
Yelled from the stands when Brendan was being overpowered in football and later thanked Chris Rabideau.
Cared for Snickers through multiple surgeries and balance issues.
Fired Janice after learning she had been stealing from Barbara and the boys.
Loved being read to as a child and treasured early books given by family.
Visited the library every Saturday and was proud of her library card.
Read widely across fiction, history, mystery, memoir, and audiobook formats.
Stayed up all night to read Harry Potter and the Sorcerous Stone when it arrived late from Amazon.
Was influenced in later reading by recommendations connected to grandchildren.
Loved the Beatles since the early sixties and even enjoyed Yellow Submarine enough to see the movie.
Collected and listened to albums by many artists across several genres.
Associated Elvis Presley’s music with Aunt Pat playing his records.
Saw Simon and Garfunkel at Towson State in a small auditorium when they were first getting started.
Says Bradley Cooper and Lady Gaga’s performance of Shallow stands out to her.
Drank vodka in college, including a trip to Ocean City with Jan Sneering.
Consumed wine regularly with John during early years in Port Townsend and Kelso.
Stopped drinking wine due to migraines and eventually became a teetotaler.
Occasionally drinks champagne for special occasions.
Prefers chai tea lattes as a favorite beverage.
Recalls Brendan telling a joke that made her laugh, though she cannot remember the details.
Describes family members as her most precious possessions.
Retains numerous inherited items from parents and biological mother.
Shares memories of childhood trips and family traditions.
Details gifts and items associated with children and grandchildren.
Reflects on emotional value of family mementos throughout her home.
Remembers enjoying her mother's meatloaf as a child.
Describes current preference for simple bowl meals.
Expresses strong appreciation for seafood growing up in Maryland.
Describes foods she disliked as a child and ways she avoided eating them.
Shares experiences traveling and enjoying meals in Finland and various international cuisines.
Recalls trying traditional foods in Scotland and disliking them.
Describes humorous memory of becoming intoxicated during a multi-course meal.
Describes John as optimistic and central to her happiness.
Finds joy in supporting her children, grandchildren, and extended family.
Maintains daily communication with friends recovering from strokes.
Participates in church ministries including quilting, bereavement, and charitable giving.
Creates and donates quilts, prayer shawls, and crafts for family and community.
Paints rocks and distributes them to bring joy to others.
Finds happiness in acts of service and spiritual life.

Rejects most traditional superstitions while acknowledging small playful ones.
Compares cruise travel with bus tours and their advantages.
Describes multiple international trips with family and groups.
Highlights experiences in Alaska, South America, Europe, and Oceania.
Recalls traveling with extended family members on several trips.
Describes detailed travel experiences in Peru, Ecuador, and the Galapagos.
Participated in hiking, snorkeling, and cultural visits.
Describes wildlife encounters and natural environments.
Recalls John stepping in turtle dung and being bitten by fire ants.
Reflects on favorite travel destinations and experiences.
Expresses desire to revisit certain locations.
Recalls group travel experiences with family and friends.
Imagines witnessing events from the life of Jesus.
Expresses admiration for Winston Churchill during WWII.
Draws comparison to modern leadership.
Considers but ultimately rejects the idea of knowing the future.

Lists family members as primary recipients.

Describes ideal lazy day activities including reading, crafts, and relaxing.
Discusses genetic predisposition to hair loss.
Reflects on family medical history.
Describes diagnosis of scoliosis from childhood.
Believes the ultimate purpose of life is to reach heaven with God.
Believes each person has a predetermined plan and life path set by God.
Emphasizes making choices aligned with discovering one’s mission in life.
Wants to be remembered as someone who improved the lives of others.
Reflects on environmental changes over her lifetime.
Desires to be remembered for her roles within family and community.

Born on President Abraham Lincoln's birthday (12 Feb 1948).
Biological mother Emily Schriefer died 24 Oct 1950 when Barbara was 2.5 years old (memoir p.13 — precise date confirmed).

1952, 12 Apr: Ethel Quinn Schriefer died; Barbara (age 4) and Chuck (age 5) moved to live with Ethel's brother John Joseph Quinn and wife Marie Ellinghaus-Quinn on Nicklas Avenue. Quinn household had four children: Margaret 'Peggy' (nursing school), Joan (telephone operator), John, and Pat (teenagers).
Marie Ellinghaus-Quinn became Barbara's functional 'Grandmother Marie' — 'the wisest person I've known' (memoir p.57).

Emily's insurance policy feud: Emily's first husband Jack Poleman (naval aviator shot down on D-Day) left a policy naming Emily as beneficiary. Emily redirected it to her brothers Kenneth and George Schriefer Jr. before marrying Buckey, then never updated. After Emily's 1950 death, brothers took the money — causing Buckey's lifelong falling-out with his brothers-in-law (memoir p.13-14).
1963, 22 Nov: Heard JFK assassination news in the classroom.
1964, 9 Feb: First day of high school at Mercy High School, Baltimore.

Teaching career: 7th grade Meridian MS (1970s) → St. Rose School Kelso WA → Lower Columbia College (tutor, Testing Coordinator) → University of Portland → Crownpoint NM high school (Study Skills, English, AP monitor, film/cinema elective).
1972: Son Brian born in Meridian MS. KKK active in Meridian — woke up to crosses visible on front lawns.
CORRECTION CONFIRMED: Miss Maryland 1968 / Miss World USA 1969 titles belong to PAULETTE RECK, Barbara's Mercy High School classmate — NOT Barbara. Corrected in timeline 18 Apr 2026.

Barbara designs her own quilts, including an Australian-themed quilt inspired by their trip there, a complex burgundy pattern, a sun design taken from a favorite TV show, and a caricature quilt of her two sons.
Soon after moving to Ridgefield, Barbara made a quilt for the new baby of the family who owned their local Mexican restaurant, El Rancho Viejo, and she has been greeted with hugs there ever since.

The Army-Navy weekend when she and John first talked about marriage was at the end of November 1968. John's parents George and Beryl came, along with Ralph, Rosemary and Louise O'Dell, Pete and Betty O'Neil, and the O'Donalds. Barbara shared a hotel room with Uncle Ralph and Aunt Rosemary. Army won 21-14.
She and John went diamond shopping in Annapolis in February 1969, after the Army-Navy weekend.
One of her students at Kate Griffin Junior High was Brenda Chaney, sister of civil-rights worker James Chaney, who was murdered by the Klan for registering black voters.

Her running career began with Port Townsend's Rhodie Run; with friends Brent and Rosemary Shirley the family took a replica Victorian house float to parades around the Northwest for the Port Townsend Queen's Court, and she later ran the Gilroy Garlic Festival race.

In 1993 Barbara and John took an Alaskan cruise with Granny and Pops (her father and stepmother) and Nana and Bob, including a helicopter ride to the Mendenhall Glacier and a train ride up into the gold fields.
In 2012 Barbara and John took a bus tour of Ireland and the Continent, staying in Dublin, Vienna, Salzburg, the Black Forest and Paris.
In 2015 Barbara and John took a Caribbean cruise that sailed from Fort Lauderdale.
In 2016 Barbara and John took an ocean cruise around South America, starting with Iguazu Falls and Buenos Aires, visiting the Falklands and Patagonia and rounding the tip of the continent.
In 2017 Barbara and John went to Mont Blanc to watch Brendan race the UTMB, then took a bus tour of Spain, Portugal and Gibraltar.

Barbara and John spent their 20th wedding anniversary on Maui; their other Hawaii trips included stays at the Hale Koa Hotel on Oahu, a Christmas trip, a whole-family trip, and trips with Trudy and with George and Cindy.

Barbara's heirlooms include a black-and-gold rocking chair that was Grandmother Quinn's wedding present, her brother Chuck's youth chair, and a pewter tea set her parents gave on their fifth wedding anniversary; John gave her a miniature Naval Academy class ring.

As a child Barbara went with her family to a Quaker family's furniture barn in Pennsylvania, where her parents chose the wood and design for two end tables and a coffee table, and the children drank sassafras root beer.

Barbara joined John in New Mexico about two years after he moved there for work. (about 2005)
Barbara and John moved back from New Mexico to Ridgefield, WA, in 2010, arriving in the Vancouver area that January.
Right after the 31 Jan 1970 wedding she moved to Milton, Florida, John's first duty station. The drive there was their only honeymoon. They moved five times in their first three years of marriage.
Next they lived in Beeville, Texas, in an unfinished house that the owner, Henry Isler, let them have rent free if they fixed it up. Navy couple Cindy and Bob Riera lived next door. (about 1970)

In Meridian, Mississippi, she team-taught science and English at Kate Griffin Junior High. She got pregnant with Brian that summer and was let go because pregnant teachers were not allowed. (about 1971-1972)
The family lived in Oak Harbor for two years while John flew from the USS Ranger. Barbara sat on the board of Brian's preschool and volunteered there two or three days a week.
They lived in Port Townsend for two and a half years after John left active duty. (about 1976-1978)
They lived in Gilroy, California, for 18 months. At the same time her brother Chuck was at postgraduate school in Monterey. (about 1978-1979)

In Vancouver, Washington, they rented at first and then bought a Victorian house next to the WSU campus. When John took the New Mexico job they sold it, and Barbara lived in an apartment in Vancouver before joining him in Crownpoint.

The family lived about one year in Redding, California, then moved back to the Pacific Northwest to an apartment in Vancouver, Washington; their dog Snickers died in 1996 while they were still in Redding. (about 1995-1996)

During her roughly three years as Running Start coordinator at Lower Columbia College she lived in Ridgefield, Washington, and commuted to Longview, while John worked away (driving truck, consulting, then in New Mexico). (about 2002-2005)
She finished her quarter at Lower Columbia College and joined John in Crownpoint, New Mexico, in March 2005, after they had lived apart for two to three years.

When the Navy sent John to Beeville with 'no dependents' housing, they stayed two days in a hotel, then with a classmate of John's, then rented an unfinished house from landlord Henry Isler, finishing it in exchange for three months' free rent; she says they survived Hurricane Camille there. (about 1970)
education: The research trip around Washington for her master's thesis (Master of Arts, Seattle Pacific) happened when Brendan was ten and Brian thirteen, which puts it around summer 1985.
Barbara lists the University of Portland among the schools she attended, alongside St. Dominic's, Mercy High, Towson State and Seattle Pacific.
career: Barbara and John both retired at 62, as they had planned (about 2010 for Barbara).
While at Lower Columbia College she taught a U.S. Government class at night to high school students, and also taught INDV 90, How To Succeed in College.

She was hired in the University of Portland School of Education after interviewing with Ellyn Arwood, who became her boss, and Dean Sister Maria, and worked there about two years in the outreach master's program. (about 1996-1998)

At Crownpoint High School she was hired on the spot by the long-time principal Mr. (Bruce) Helms and worked four years under him; after he retired she stayed one more year and left when her five years were up in March. (2005-about 2010)

people.name: Charles Buckey McKeldin
notable_stories: Maintained a lifelong family feud with his brothers-in-law over an insurance policy payout after his first wife's death
Ice cream delivery during college
Lifelong falling-out with brothers-in-law (Kenneth and George Schriefer Jr.) over Emily's insurance policy payout after her 1950 death (memoir p. 13-14)

CORRECTION: Family lore of 'four sisters Lola/Lillian/Helen/Emma + brother Billy' as Buckey's siblings likely refers to his AUNTS AND UNCLES (Charles E McKeldin I's siblings), not Buckey's own siblings. Buckey had siblings from his mother Emma Bell McKeldin — these are yet to be confirmed from records.
His sisters called him 'Buckey'. His wife (Barbara's stepmother Peggy) hated the nickname and once said on the drive home from a visit that she would be sick if she heard 'Buckey' one more time.

He took the children to Orioles and Colts games, the Ringling Brothers circus and Barbara's Saturday duckpin bowling, and took them fishing on the Chesapeake Bay at Ocean City. Sunday country drives ended with ice cream if they behaved.
Brian and Brendan called him Pops (with Peggy as Granny).
Buckey and Peggy visited the Adamses out west every other year, came for both boys' First Communions, and stayed at their Kelso house for Mike and Shelley's wedding.
The family called him 'Pops', and he and Peggy were 'Granny and Pops' to the grandchildren.

He went to the Duck Carvers Convention in Ocean City and always came back with bird pins or decoys; he carved a few himself, including a swan and a Santa, and at his death Barbara split his decoys with her brothers.
With Peggy he went on the 1993 Alaska cruise with Barbara and John, and on a Hawaii trip with them and Nana that took in Oahu, Maui and the Big Island.
His favourite tree was the dogwood, and he gave Barbara a pinkie ring engraved with her initials BJM.

people.name: George Francis Adams Sr.
personality: Did not bring his work home
Prioritized his wife Beryl above all else
The most important thing in his life was my Mom
notable_stories: A professional military law enforcement officer (Provost Marshall) who did not bring his work home and prioritized his wife, Beryl, above all else
Drafted for WWII: MP, self-defense instructor, Commander of POW camp holding Japanese combatants in Hawaii
Recalled for Korean War: Commander of MP detachment in Okinawa

Postings: Presidio SF (1954), Ft. Gordon GA, Frankfurt/Heidelberg (1958–62), Presidio SF (1962–), South Korea (13 months unaccompanied), retired as Provost Marshall of Ft. Lewis / Eastern Washington (1971)
1930 census listed as George F. Wells, step-son — Arthur Wells was his step-father
Arthur died when John was in 11th grade (~1963-64); Nini then moved in with John's family in San Francisco until her own death in 1967
Prior career included Union Oil / Standard Oil truck driver and St. Martin's College Olympia
Recorded correctly as step-child with surname Adams on the 1930 census (not Wells)
Cause of death confirmed: cancer, 'probably self-inflicted' — he was a moderate smoker and daily drinker (John's memoir).
He was a 'prototypical, Greatest Generation Soldier.'
Drafted first for WWII, then recalled for the Korean Conflict. After that he decided to make the Army his career.
WWII: served in Hawaii as a Military Police Officer, self-defense instructor, and Commander of a POW camp holding Japanese combatants.
Korean Conflict: Commander of the Military Police detachment in Okinawa.
First Presidio SF assignment (1954): attended San Francisco State University and finished his college degree; in charge of the stockade.
Germany (1958-62): in charge of the Military Police who rode the German trains.
Back at Presidio SF (1962): administrative job as coordinator of industrial defense on the west coast.
South Korea: assigned Provost Marshall of South Korea, went unaccompanied for 13 months.
Final assignment: Provost Marshall of Ft. Lewis and Eastern Washington, retired 1971.
Started taking family movies in Okinawa, sporadically continued through John's high school years.
At one point he told John: 'Don't expect praise. If they aren't dumping on you, you are doing just fine.'

The 1930 census taker wrongly recorded him as George F. Wells, though his relationship to the head of household was correctly given as stepson. His siblings Presley and Edith were correctly listed as stepchildren surnamed Adams.
A family photo of George and Serena shows their son (George Sr.) at about 3 years old, taken shortly before his father's death in 1920.
At the Presidio he was promoted and ran the stockade, so prisoners mowed the lawn at the family's quarters; the family got its first television and he never missed the Friday Night Fights.
When a typhoon was coming in on Okinawa, he took young John and George out into the yard and ran holding their hands while they flapped in the wind behind him.
When John was accused of breaking windows with a slingshot in Germany, his father made him prove it wasn't him ('Just the facts, mister'), which taught John to stay out of trouble.
On visits to the Simons farm in Pasco he fished the Columbia River, catching big steelhead.

On a rare fishing trip together, John tried to net a big salmon his father had fought for fifteen minutes, flipped it into the air, and it broke the line and swam off. Dad barely spoke on the way home, never told the story, and never asked John to go fishing again. Everyone else found it hilarious.
He once took both sons, John and George, for 18 holes at the Ft. Lewis Golf Course; they struggled so badly that he never asked them again.
George Sr. was a golfer who played early perimeter-weighted Lynx clubs. He was set on making John a golfer and took him, and sometimes his brother George Jr., out to the course.
George and Beryl went to the 1968 Army-Navy game weekend in Philadelphia with John and Barbara. George, an Army man, was pleased when Army won 21-14.
George Sr. was Papa to his grandsons Brian and Brendan, who spent Christmases at Nana and Papa's with cousins George, Geoffrey, Chris and Camille; he took the boys out in his boat on Puget Sound.

On the day Mount St. Helens erupted, Papa, Nana, Aunt Rosemary and Uncle Ralph drove down for Brian's First Communion; hearing the Toutle River had flooded I-5, they left at once for Olympia, and Papa talked the authorities into letting them through.
Papa made cider from the apple trees in his and Nana's front yard.

Per Dale Morrow's Hamilton research, several of her siblings moved to Darke County, Ohio in the very early 1800s. [Bill Allen, Further Research, 2012, line 7356]
The 1850 census shows her living with the Gills, alongside a Sam'l Peer [Bill Allen, Further Research, 2012, line 8691]
Had at least one daughter and one son [Bill Allen, Further Research, 2012, line 9674]

Bill Allen’s hypothesis: Bill thinks she probably remarried soon after Jose died; no record of a remarriage has been found. [Bill Allen, line 4019]
Sources disagree: The 1850 census age suggests she was born about 1783, in Virginia. [Bill Allen, line 7497]

The family (and Bill's Uncle Ralph) long believed Gavin Hamilton of Mauchline was Eliza's father and sent her to Harper's Ferry, but the dates showed he was too old. [Family research emails, email 42]
Research lead (Francis Hamilton): A Francis Hamilton married Sarah Lee in 1818; the license was signed by Jose Adams. [Family research emails, email 41]
Research lead (Francis Hamilton): Francis Hamilton, Eliza's brother, was a close friend of Jose Adams. [Family research emails, email 41]
Research lead (Gill): In 1850 a Gill family in Licking County, Ohio, had Elizabeth Adams (76) living with them; Bill thinks one of her daughters married into it. [Family research emails, email 08]
Research lead (Samuel Peer): Samuel Peer, aged 19, was in the Gill household with Elizabeth Adams in the 1850 census. [Family research emails, email 08]
Research lead (Francis Hamilton): Francis Hamilton married a woman named Eliza (surname unknown). [Family research emails, email 20]
Research lead (Francis Hamilton): Francis Hamilton and his sister Mary owned a foundry in Harpers Ferry. [Family research emails, email 20]
Research lead (Francis Hamilton): The family holds a copy of Francis Hamilton's will, which left a small sum to the young George Francis Adams. [Family research emails, email 20]

Unconfirmed: Bill Allen suspects she is buried in Luray Cemetery, but no record has been found. [Family research emails, email 13]

people.name: Gavin Hamilton of Mauchline
notable_stories: Friend and patron of the poet Robert Burns. From Martinmas 1784 he sublet Mossgiel farm to Robert and Gilbert Burns, urged Robert to publish his poems by subscription, and was the dedicatee of the 1786 Kilmarnock edition.
In March 1788 he asked Burns to stand guarantor for a large sum owed by Gilbert Burns; Burns declined, but the friendship survived.
His house and office beside the churchyard at Mauchline were nicknamed "the Castle".

Robert Burns’s first book, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (the Kilmarnock volume, printed by John Wilson, 31 July 1786, 600 copies), was dedicated to him. Burns, short of money for a passage to the West Indies, published by subscription at his suggestion.
milestones: Buried in Mauchline kirkyard; at his request there was no headstone, and the Partick Burns Club placed a plaque on his grave in 1919
Religion: a "New Licht" liberal, pursued by the Rev. William "Daddy" Auld and the Kirk Session; the Presbytery of Ayr found in his favour (25 June 1785)
career: Trained in his father’s law office, then practised as a writer (lawyer) in Mauchline, where he was known as "The Clerk"
Factor to the Earl of Loudoun, from whom he leased Mossgiel farm
Collector of the stent, the Kirk Session’s poor-relief levy (1775)

people.name: John Howard Adams
locations: Germany; France; Spain; Austria; Switzerland; Great Britain; Berlin
NAS Pensacola, FL; USS Lexington, Gulf of Mexico
personality: Tried to be kind, understanding, generous and demonstrative
notable_stories: Delivered Barbara’s sack lunch to Lowell when he was near Port Townsend on Reserve weekend.
Initially became a 'Catholic of convenience' to simplify marrying a Catholic.
Has maintained a friendship with Kevin Finnegan.
Did not like sharing Barbara with other suitors in Baltimore.
Asked Barbara's father for permission to marry her.
Proposed to Barbara in the basement of her house.
Moved frequently with Barbara during Navy life and later civilian work.
Drove truck for a while after being downsized.
Built a plywood platform over the back seating area for the trip.
Pulled over during Brian's diaper blowout.
Went to Survival School and lost 13 pounds in a week.
Went into the emergency room with Brendan while Barbara waited outside.
Later took Brian to the hospital for his injury.
Reassured Barbara that Brian would be okay.
Provided his own favorite songs list within the artifact.
Blue and Gold admissions officer for USNA
Honeymoon: Drove Annapolis → Pensacola FL for continued flight training
Best Man at wedding: Willie Durkin — John's high school best friend from San Francisco, career SF firefighter, Navy Corpsman at NAS Jacksonville. Died 2021, Alzheimer's complications.

Proposal to Barbara: After the 1968 Army-Navy game, Philadelphia, PA. Conversation-based (no ring, no knee); 'O'Neils, O'Donnels, O'Dells and O'Adams' entourage in hotel room. John subsequently asked Buckey, who replied: 'What makes you think you can support her in the manner she is accustomed on an Ensign's salary in the Navy?' John's starting salary was $345/month plus flight pay.

Engagement ring: 1/2-karat VVS stone bought in Annapolis. Presented to Barbara asleep in the basement of her Baltimore home (Nov 1968). Rating upgraded to 'Flawless' over decades through re-mountings.
Barbara also has a pinky-finger miniature Naval Academy ring with aquamarine stones cut from the same stone as John's Academy ring.
Wedding ring briefly lost playing softball in Port Townsend; replaced by Barbara with a narrower band.
Name origin: John probably after John Kulp (mother's grandfather) or John Wesley Adams (Gen 3). Howard after mother's favorite brother Howard (whose real name was Byron Daniel).
Named 'Howard' after Beryl's favorite brother Byron Daniel 'Howard' Simons (mem).
1952: First big trip — to Okinawa with family.
1954: First family television set; first family car was a used 1949 DeSoto, kept until 1959 departure for Germany.
1964: San Francisco City High School football championship — his school won.
1976: Left active duty, joined Navy Reserves as XO, Aviation Maintenance Division, NAS Whidbey Island.
1978: Transitioned to civilian paper industry (engineering, project management, logistics).
1980: Father George Francis Adams Sr. died.
1995: Left Crown (Crown Zellerbach / Crown Pacific); moved to Redding, CA.

NOTE: This source again reports Beryl's death as 1999 (memoir ~p.136: 'would have turned 80 that Christmas Day'). User has previously confirmed 1998-08-01 as correct canonical date — maintaining 1998. Both memoir sources (this + Adams_Direct_Line) report 1999.
2009: Retired at age 62.
Present (2026): Lives between Ridgefield WA and Englewood CO.
Navy call sign: 'Quincy' — but not routinely used as a nickname.

Mid-air collision off USS Ranger: A-6 Intruder struck by F-4 Phantom wingman whose squadron commander had crossed through the carrier's landing pattern. Cockpit fire; aircraft tumbled. John ejected, failed to release parachute on water entry, pulled underwater twice, finally activated strobe light on helmet, picked up within a minute. Bombardier also ejected — cracked neck, more severely burned. (Memoir p.99-102.)
First boss in civilian world: Lowell Tiller, a consummate Mechanical Engineer; Lowell died early from MS. His wife Lillian and Barbara are close friends to this day.
On August 14, 2021, met a 60-year-old cousin for the very first time.
Applied to all service academies; originally received West Point appointment but requested Annapolis as first choice. Father (in South Korea) was somewhat surprised.
Father's advice staying at USNA: 'Well, if you do that, what do you think you'll do with yourself?' — kept John from leaving halfway through Plebe Year.

Career: State of New Mexico school construction financing in Crownpoint, NM. Position came through son Brendan, who was working for Gerald Martin General Contractor and introduced a State of New Mexico representative to John — John was hired as construction manager for public schools in the north-central part of the state.
Grew up at the Presidio in San Francisco, where his father was a military police officer, and went to high school with O.J. Simpson.
In summer 2010 John was about to take a trip and was mainly interested in the family's Scottish connection. His brother George sent him material on Gavin Hamilton and Robert Burns.
John and Barbara travelled to Scotland with his sister Trudy in 2010.
The family flew home from Frankfurt to New York on a 707 in 1962, picked up a new Dodge and drove across the country by a southern route.

After John finished 4th grade in 1958, the family spent about a month camping across the country from Pasco through Idaho and South Dakota to Georgia, seeing Coeur d'Alene, Mount Rushmore, Yellowstone and the Smoky Mountains; it was the longest stretch of daily time the children ever had with their father.

While living in Germany John first skied in Switzerland, saw the Passion Play at Oberammergau, toured East Berlin before the Wall was built, spent two weeks on the Spanish Riviera, and as a Boy Scout visited Great Britain.
In high school John rode his 15-speed French touring bike from San Francisco to the Russian River and camped on property owned by Mike Remy's family.

John began playing baseball at 7, often on more than one team at once, and stopped after his second year of college; at 15-16 he played on three Bay Area teams and was named league MVP playing catcher and pitcher.
John played center on the 1964 San Francisco City champion high school football team and was named to the All-City team; the team played against future stars O.J. Simpson and Mike Holmgren.

On his summer cruise out of Norfolk, John's ship collided with a fleet tug playing an enemy ship in a war-at-sea exercise; it went into dry dock in Baltimore, Barbara's home town, so he spent most weekends that summer with her.
John bought a car over Christmas break of his senior year, against Academy rules, and kept it hidden; most weekends Barbara came to Annapolis or he went to Baltimore.
A few people called John 'Howie', from his middle name, but it never lasted because the family moved so often.

John never golfed with his father, joking that golf wasn't a sport because you didn't tape your ankles, but took it up with his father's clubs; he played Pebble Beach twice in the late 1980s, made a hole-in-one in a 2001 company tournament at Heron Lakes Golf Course in Portland, OR, and was once paired with Cheech Marin at the Presidio course.

John's lasting high school friends included Susie Miller, Kendall Price and Mark Peterson, who followed him to the Naval Academy; he spent a week with Susie's family on Lake Michigan in summer 1967 and took her to that year's Army-Navy Game.
Plebe Year was the worst year of his life: he was hazed constantly and fought to keep a C average, since anything lower meant probation or dismissal.

Once during the engagement Barbara took off her ring outside a movie theater, put it in John's shirt pocket and said she didn't think she wanted to go through with it; later that evening she took it back out of his pocket.
He still has the original Navy 'Wings of Gold' that Barbara pinned on him when he earned them as a carrier pilot.

The Rolex his parents gave him for his 1965 high-school graduation vanished in about 1973; a couple of years later friends in the Philippines mailed it back after finding it behind the cushions of a sofa set they had bought from John and Barbara. A jeweler later found it was made in 1958, so his father probably bought it in Korea.
He was offered the job of Mill Manager in Carthage, New York, when Brian was about to start his senior year of high school and Brendan his freshman year, and turned it down for the family's sake.
His mother taught him to iron and to cook when he was in about seventh grade; he has done most of the family's ironing ever since and cooks most evening meals in retirement.

After his father died, his mother let the children choose keepsakes and John took his father's pocket knife. He later lost it, Brendan tried to replace it one Christmas, and John finally found the same model.

As Logistics Manager at Wauna he won a weekend at a Columbia Gorge bed and breakfast in a trucking company's golf-tournament drawing; he and Barbara used it for their anniversary and went skiing on Mt. Hood.
Family and friends call John by the pet names "Papa" (to his grandchildren), "Johnboy" and "Best Buddy".
John played organized baseball from age 7 until his second year of college, often on two teams at once, and played every position except first base and the outfield.

When his high-school baseball glove was stolen from the bench during batting practice, John had to buy a replacement from his own savings; he named it "Mr. Mitt," and the glove still survives almost 60 years later in Colorado.
After his father died, John took the gift of his father's golf clubs as a sign to take the game seriously, and went on to play more than a thousand rounds over 40-plus years.
During the pandemic John made hard-bound photo books of their international trips, and he makes a photo book for each grandchild's 16th birthday.
John and Barbara planned a Hawaii vacation for the whole extended family together, and they have made about ten trips to Hawaii, visiting all of the islands.

John and Barbara found the Cadillac Cafe near Lloyd Center in Portland around 1982, just after it opened. They stayed regulars for as long as it existed, and on their 45th anniversary visit, probably in 2015, the owners told them they had sold it.
John and Barbara celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary with the whole family at El Rancho Viejo, their regular Mexican restaurant in Ridgefield.
John became 'Uncle Hims' after his niece Jenny, Chuck's daughter, whom he and Barbara babysat over a long weekend, told her parents tearfully, 'Hims sent me to my room.'

One Saturday night in Kelso, already dressed in suit and tie for a formal dinner, John took the training wheels off Brendan's bike and ran up and down the road with him until he balanced; they still arrived on time.
John collects Hard Rock Cafe T-shirts from locations around the world; on the 2016 South America trip the tour guide let him off at a Hard Rock Cafe to get one.
At the Equator in Ecuador, John was the only one in the tour group who could balance an egg on the head of a nail, earning the title 'Egg Master'.
In Dublin, Barbara saved John's life twice when he looked the wrong way before crossing the street.
In retirement John golfs, goes to the driving range weekly, meets with two coffee groups each week, swims at 24 Hour Fitness, does the food shopping and makes dinner.

As a small child John lived in Richmond and Sacramento, California, while his father worked for Union Oil after leaving the Army after WWII. (before 1952)
In 1952, when his father left for Okinawa, John, his mother and siblings lived in Pasco, Washington, near his mother's family until they could join him.
The family lived for almost two years in military housing in the town of Naha, Okinawa, with blackout shutters on the windows; John started school there. (1952 to about 1954)
John lived at the Presidio in San Francisco for his 1st through 4th grades (1954-1958), during his father's first assignment there.

On returning from Germany in 1962 (John's 9th grade), the family first lived in a flat in the Richmond District of San Francisco before getting housing on the Presidio, later in senior officers' quarters whose back yard was a fairway of the Presidio golf course.
John and Barbara arrived in Washington State in 1972.
After seven years in New Mexico, John and Barbara moved back to Ridgefield, WA (this passage gives his retirement as 2010; the summary chapter says 2009).

While living in Germany he toured France, Spain, Austria and Switzerland with his family, went to Great Britain with the Boy Scouts, and rode the trains through East Germany to the divided city of Berlin. (1960-1961)
The family came back to San Francisco in 1962 and lived on the Presidio until 1965, when he finished high school.
The family was living in Oak Harbor, Washington, in about 1973.
Before moving to New Mexico, John and Barbara lived in the 'blue house' in Ridgefield, Washington. (late 1990s)
Over the two years after the Rexam job ended, John drove a long-haul truck while still living in Vancouver, WA, and then moved to New Mexico for work. (about 2001-2003)
John and Barbara came back from New Mexico to the Vancouver area in January 2010 and settled in Ridgefield, WA, that year.
education: In high school John was a diver on the swim team, ran for class officer, was active in student government, played on at least three sports teams and belonged to a social club.

At the Naval Academy John played NCAA baseball and lightweight football for two years, boxed in the Plebe winter tournament, and with his handball partner reached the late rounds of the Brigade handball championship.
John earned his MBA at the University of Portland while working at a paper mill.

In high school (about 3,000 students, overlooking the Bay) he was class president twice (including senior class president), student body president, captain of several teams, a football and baseball player, MVP of his summer Babe Ruth baseball league, and prom king at his senior prom.
He earned his MBA at the University of Portland after about three years of part-time study begun roughly 14 years after his Naval Academy degree, while working at the Wauna Mill.
John earned his MBA by taking evening classes while he worked.
career: John was retired by 2011.

After 19 years with his first paper company, John took a management job with another paper company that was soon sold; he stayed in Redding working as a consultant, then became an Engineering Manager for another paper company in Vancouver, WA, which was also later sold. (about 1995-2000)
His first job was as a paperboy for the San Francisco Chronicle, which he kept until he left for Annapolis. (before June 1965)
On leaving active duty in 1976 he became a Mechanical Engineer with Crown Zellerbach Paper Company in Port Townsend, and he and Barbara bought their first home, on a hill overlooking the town.

In 1978 he took a fast-track management job with Crown Zellerbach's Containerboard Division and moved the family to Gilroy, California; when the promises weren't kept he moved back to the Paper Division.

He then took an engineering job at the Wauna Mill outside Clatskanie, Oregon, and the family lived in Kelso, Washington, for about 16 years; he later became Logistics Manager at Wauna and rose to Superintendent. The company went from Crown Zellerbach to James River to Fort Howard over those years. (c. 1979-1995)
In 1995 he left after 19 years to take a management job with Simpson Paper Company in Redding, California; six months later Simpson sold his division and the new owners let the managers go.

After Simpson he joined a consulting company teaching ways to improve human performance, and turned down an interview for a Mill Manager job in Michigan; over the next five years he held two more jobs, including long-haul trucking. (c. 1995-2000)
He drove long-haul truck for Swift in 2001 and accepted his State of New Mexico job over the phone while driving somewhere in Montana.

He worked for the New Mexico Public School Facilities Authority, managing state funding and overseeing construction and maintenance for over 50 public schools in west-central New Mexico, including the Navajo, Zuni and Acoma reservations, Grants, Gallup and Crownpoint, with his office in Crownpoint. (2000 or 2001-c. 2010)

John worked for James River Corporation in the paper industry; on a company visit to its St. Francisville paper mill near Baton Rouge he learned his one party trick, making two wine corks appear to pass through each other.

In 2001 John was Plant Engineer for the paper company Rexam in North Portland; when Rexam sold the plant to a competitor, his engineering job was cut and he managed the graveyard shift until the handover.

notes: Born 15 Oct 1818 in England (Find a Grave; the 1860 and 1870 censuses give England, about 1818); died 30 Jun 1890 in Williams County, Ohio. Married "Mary Marsh" as Henry Symons on 24 Apr 1845 in Summit County, Ohio.

The family was at Coventry, Summit County, Ohio, in 1850 (Henry 29, Mary 32, Sarah, Isabella, George A. and the infant Aaron); at Richland Township, DeKalb County, Indiana (post office Auburn), in 1860, with Richard, Ann and Olive added; and at Northwest Township, Williams County, Ohio, in 1870. Aaron grew up in Indiana, which is why his son Ray gave his father's birthplace as Indiana in 1918.

Lead: some Ancestry trees place his birth at Berrynarbor, Devon, and name his parents William Henry Simmons (1763–1847) and Mary Pestell (1779–1857). No baptism or other record has been found to support this.
Henry Simons's will names his wife Mary and nine children: Mary Jane, Sarah, Isabell, Harriet Emma, Aaron, Richard, George A., Ann Rebecca and Olive Catherine.

His will, made 17 Mar 1889 in Northwest Township, left his property to his wife Mary while she remained his widow (she died first, in Dec 1889); thirty acres of section 15 to "Mary A. Simons, wife of Richard Simons"; five dollars each to his daughters Mary Jane, Sarah, Isabell and Emma and his sons Aaron and Richard; and the rest in equal shares to George A., Ann Rebecca and Olive Catharine. When it was proved at Bryan on 23 Jul 1890, notice went to the next of kin living in Ohio: Ann R. Forester, Olive C. Decker, Mary J. Fryman and a Rachel Simons (not identified). Witnesses: R. K. and J. M. Haughey.
In the 1880 census he was 62, a farmer in North West Township, Williams County, Ohio, both his parents born in England; the index lists him alone, and his son George lived nearby (dwelling 209).

locations: Covert Township, Van Buren County, Michigan
notable_stories: Eloped with Dradie Kulp to Ritzville in 1915
He later worked in real estate and convinced several Kulp relatives to relocate to the Tri-Cities area
Founded the Chetzamoka Park Zoo on the Columbia River waterfront (Pasco area)
Ray and Dradie celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary at the Pasco Grange
Eloped with Dradie Kulp to Ritzville; real estate developer who named streets in Pasco after family
Grandpa Ray Simons had a bout with tuberculosis, which is why they sold their Lynden farm and moved to the drier climate of Pasco, Washington in the 1950s (John's memoir — 'My Grandparents' chapter).
Ray founded the Chetzamoka Park Zoo by rescuing unwanted animals from zoos in Seattle, Portland, and Spokane.
Ray named streets in the Pasco area after family members. 'Glen Acres' is a residential development named after Beryl's brother Glen.
John's last vivid memory of Ray: mid-1970s, obviously suffering from dementia when he visited John's family in Olympia.
Ray passed away not long after the mid-1970s visit (confirmed consistent with death 7 May 1977).

His grandson Steve Simons, aged about 8 to 10, drove Ray’s pickup into Pasco with his cousin John Adams to collect discarded grocery-store food for the zoo animals, with blocks on the pedals and looking under the steering wheel. [John Howard Adams, A Memoir, text lines 190–193, 616–619]
C-005: WWI Draft Card — Birth: June 14, 1897, Michigan. Consistent with canonical.
1900 Census: Raymond Simons, age 2 (born ~1897-98). Siblings listed: Ettie, Lola, Bertha.
1920 Census — Raymond's own household: Raymond Simons (22), Dradie Simons (21), Elaine Simons (1). Elaine born ~1919.
1930 Census: Raymond and Dradie with multiple children; Elmer Kulp (Dradie's brother) present.
Simons, McPhail, and Kulp families were located within a few farms of each other prior to marriage.
John's first memory of Ray is of him chasing John's father around the farmyard with a pair of pants smeared with cow manure that George Sr. had tricked him into sitting on.
milestones: Registered for the WWI draft while working in Milton, Oregon
Moved his family from the Lynden farm to Pasco, Washington, in the 1950s
Moved family from Lynden to Pasco due to tuberculosis diagnosis
Military: Raymond Zell Simons registered for the WWI draft on 26 Aug 1918 at Blaine, Whatcom County, giving birth 14 June 1897 at South Haven, Michigan and father's birthplace Indiana.
Ray's Pasco farm had about half a mile of Columbia River waterfront, bought before the Hanford Nuclear Reservation was built; the land became valuable as the area grew. (1950s)
Late in life Ray and Dradie moved into a nursing home, and the farmland was sold. (late 1970s)
Registered for the WWII draft on 16 Feb 1942 at Kennewick, Washington; self-employed, with his brother-in-law Dan Groves as next of kin

Ray sold real estate in Pasco and persuaded several Kulp families to move there. (abt 1954)
Farmer: a rented farm at Lynden in 1920, his own farm near Richland in 1940, and a farm in Franklin County in 1950.
School bus driver in Delta, Whatcom County, in 1930.

Remarried Arthur Wells (San Francisco) after George Francis Adams' 1920 death
Moved in with John Howard Adams' family in San Francisco after Arthur Wells died (~1963-64), until her own death in 1967
After Arthur Wells died (when John was in 11th grade, ~1963-64), Nini came to live with John's family.
Nini died during John's second year at the Naval Academy (~1966-67), consistent with confirmed death date 28 Sep 1967.
John's father told him not to come home for the funeral.
She frequently wore white bobby socks around the house, saying it was 'what all the kids were wearing now-a-days.'
She would become very excited watching 'What's My Line' on television.
Had an aqua and white Hudson coupe that she and Arthur only drove when necessary.
Their apartment in downtown San Francisco had metropolitan traffic noise all night long.
Theirs was a 'yours, mine, and ours' family: Dad's siblings (Presley, Edith) from George Sr. + Nini, Rosemary Wells from Nini + Arthur, and another (Arthur's daughter from prior).
Most Easters, Arthur, Nini and George Sr.'s siblings gathered at one of their Bay Area homes and the family made a weekend of it.
Her grandson George remembers being left for the day at her downtown apartment, which bored him, but she always took him to Fisherman's Wharf to sightsee and look for toys.

media.title: The Trumbo family at their house in Chehalis, Washington, about 1891
media.caption: Page 1: the house Presley N. Trumbo built at Chehalis in 1890, with the family numbered: his father Presley at the door (1), his mother holding the baby Serena (2 and 7), and the other children on the porch and by the fence. Page 2: the key written by John Holmes Trumbo in 1957: "The old home in Chehalis built by my father in 1890. The house is still occupied and has had very few alterations." He lists his father Presley Nevil Trumbo, born 1840; his mother Hannah Lois Trumbo; himself, John Holmes Trumbo, 1881; his sisters Lizzie Buckley Trumbo, 1883, and Gertrude Trumbo, 1885; his brother Presley Nevil Trumbo, 1887; and his sister Serena Maria Nevada Trumbo.
media.source: Shared on Ancestry.com by Therese Roberson, 21 Jan 2018; from the public member tree "Turner / Harvey Family Tree".
